title: Christopher Nolan Wants His Next Film to Be a Horror Movie. The Odyssey Proves He Can Do It.
excerpt: After The Odyssey opened to a record $264 million worldwide, Nolan told The Hollywood Reporter that audiences who want horror from him should 'just buy a ticket' — and confirmed he is actively searching for the right story.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Christopher Nolan hints at making a horror film after The Odyssey's success.
  • The Odyssey opened to a record $264.1 million globally, Nolan's biggest debut.
  • Nolan's Circe sequence in The Odyssey is described as a fully fleshed-out horror scene.

  • Christopher Nolan told The Hollywood Reporter that his Circe sequence in The Odyssey already delivers horror: "They don't need to beg me to tell a horror story anymore. Just buy a ticket."
  • In a separate interview with Fred Asquith, Nolan said he would "love" to make a full horror film but is waiting for the right idea and story.
  • The Odyssey opened to $264.1 million globally — $124.5 million domestic, $139.6 million international — becoming Nolan's biggest worldwide debut ever.

Christopher Nolan has conquered science fiction, superhero cinema, war epics, and historical drama. Now, riding the massive opening weekend of The Odyssey, the Oscar-winning director is making clear what genre he wants to tackle next: horror.

"Just Buy a Ticket"

In an interview with The Hollywood Reporter, Nolan addressed the long-standing clamor from fans for a pure horror film. His response was characteristically blunt. "They don't need to beg me to tell a horror story anymore," he said. "Just buy a ticket."

He was referring to a specific sequence in The Odyssey — the Circe feeding frenzy, featuring Samantha Morton — that critics have called a fully "fleshed-out horror sequence," a first in Nolan's 25-year filmography. The scene, according to early reviews, represents a tonal departure that proves Nolan can generate genuine dread when he wants to.

But one scene is not enough for Nolan. He told the outlet that the sequence "whets my appetite for more," signaling that a full-length horror feature is firmly on his radar.

The Idea Comes First

In a longer conversation with YouTuber Fred Asquith during The Odyssey's press tour, Nolan elaborated on what has kept him from making a horror film so far. "I'd love to do a horror movie," he said. "But it's all about the idea. It's all about, is there a story that really compels you, and I've never found that for me other than in other ways."

"It's a visceral genre. It's one where you're really trying to give the audience a feeling of what the characters are experiencing. And that's the type of filmmaking I really enjoy."

— Christopher Nolan, in conversation with Fred Asquith

Nolan pointed out that darker elements have threaded through his recent work. He described Oppenheimer as, in one sense, "a horror movie" because of the darkness of its subject matter. And Homer's original Odyssey text, he noted, has "very significant elements of horror baked into" it — elements he deliberately leaned into for the film.

Nolan Praises the New Wave of Horror

Nolan is not just watching the horror genre from a distance. In an interview with The Telegraph, he praised recent horror films Backrooms and Obsession as proof that cinema "continues to transform itself." He called Backrooms evidence that young audiences are embracing mystery and ambiguity: "Parts of Backrooms are like David Lynch at his most obscure. And yet young people can't get enough of them."

On Curry Barker's Obsession, Nolan was even more emphatic. "When you go see a film like Obsession, that's an amazing idea," he told The Hollywood Reporter. "That movie works like a motherfucker. It's not about the technical side. It's about story. So I'm always looking."

The Odyssey's Record-Shattering Debut

These comments arrive with considerable weight behind them. The Odyssey opened to $264.1 million worldwide on its debut weekend — $124.5 million domestically and $139.6 million internationally across 73 markets, according to Universal Pictures and Reuters. It is Nolan's biggest global opening ever, surpassing The Dark Knight Rises ($249 million). It is also the fourth-biggest R-rated opening in domestic box office history, trailing only three Deadpool films.

The film earned an "A" CinemaScore and a 97% audience rating on Rotten Tomatoes, suggesting strong legs through August despite Spider-Man: Brand New Day arriving next weekend.

India was a standout market. The film earned $7.3 million on its opening weekend — the largest ever for a non-franchise Hollywood production in the country, according to The Wrap. IMAX tickets in Mumbai had been priced as high as ₹3,300 and sold out in advance, with the film pre-selling 1.25 lakh tickets in national chains before opening day, according to Bollywood Hungama.

What Comes Next

Nolan has not announced his next project, and he has hinted at taking time off after the exhausting production of The Odyssey, which was shot over 91 days across multiple countries and cost $250 million — his most expensive film to date. The movie stars Matt Damon as Odysseus, alongside Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya, Robert Pattinson, Charlize Theron, and Lupita Nyong'o.

But the pattern is consistent: after Oppenheimer's seven Oscar wins and nearly $1 billion at the box office, Nolan pivoted to Greek mythology rather than repeating historical drama. A pivot to horror would be equally characteristic — and given The Odyssey's Circe sequence, he has already proven the instinct is there.

For Indian audiences who filled IMAX screens from Mumbai to Delhi for The Odyssey, the prospect of a Nolan horror film is one more reason to watch what the director does next. As Nolan himself put it: the search is on.
